entries.name: North American river otter
behaviour: slides down muddy banks tail first
caches live fish in flooded dens
highly playful; chases and wrestles
entries.notes: Mating occurs about a year before birth: 9-11 months of delayed implantation, then ~60 days of true gestation. Tracks and slides along banks give it away.

entries.name: Eurasian otter
behaviour: solitary and crepuscular
travels huge home ranges along waterways
uses spraints to mark otter paths
entries.notes: Widely distributed across Eurasia and North Africa; a flagship of clean river water. Gestation includes long delayed implantation, like its American cousin.

entries.name: North American beaver
behaviour: fells trees and dams streams
builds lodges with underwater entrances
slaps flat tail on water as alarm
entries.notes: The aquatic engineer: dam-building beavers turn streams into ponds and wetlands for dozens of other species.

entries.name: Eurasian beaver
behaviour: built lodges and burrow bank dens
loud tail-slap alarm
stores winter food caches underwater
entries.notes: Nearly driven to extinction for castoreum and fur; brought back across Europe, now a common sight on slow rivers.

entries.name: Giant river otter
behaviour: noisy family clans defend lake and river stretches
unique pale throat patches used for recognition
charges caimans and anacondas when cornered
entries.notes: The loudest otter: family choruses carry across blackwater lakes. Endangered; the best-known Amazon river mammal after the boto.

entries.name: American alligator
behaviour: spring bellowing chorus
female excavates and guards the mound nest, then carries hatchlings in her jaws
temperature-dependent sex: warm eggs become males
entries.notes: gestation_days is egg incubation. Recoved from near-extinction in the US; a bellowing male at dusk is the swamp's bass note.

entries.name: Gharial
behaviour: lies motionless in deep clear pools, spearing fish with a sideways snap of the thin snout
cannot walk on land; belly-slides into the water
colonial nesters on open sandbanks; crèches of hatchlings

voxel_model.pattern: long pencil-thin snout; bulbous nasal 'ghara' on males

entries.notes: Critically endangered crocodilian of the Ganges and Brahmaputra. gestation_days is sand-nest incubation. A living fossil; model nests as shallow holes on sand.

entries.name: Great blue heron
behaviour: stands statue-still then spear-strikes
nests in noisy treetop rookeries
flies with slow deep wingbeats and folded neck
entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. The statue at every river bend; colonies visible for miles in tall cottonwoods.

entries.name: Grey heron
behaviour: stands motionless in shallows for fish
colonial treetop nester ('heronry')
returns to the same nest for years
entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. Europe's familiar heron; heronries are among the loudest bird colonies near rivers.

entries.name: Osprey
entries.migrates: migrates long distances between breeding and wintering grounds
behaviour: hover-hunts, then plunge-dives feet-first into water
carries fish head-first for aerodynamics
nests atop dead snags and nest platforms

voxel_model.pattern: dark eye stripe and white head

entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. The only fish-eating raptor with reversible outer toes; a universal near-fishing bird, worldwide.

entries.name: Mallard
behaviour: dabbles upended for plants
drakes have glossy green heads; mottled brown females
many domestic ducks descend from mallards

voxel_model.pattern: drake: iridescent green head, white neck ring

entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. The default duck of every temperate pond and river; handless to model, beloved everywhere.

entries.name: Common merganser
behaviour: dives for fish, saw-toothed serrated bill for grip
travels in lines along clear salmon rivers
nests in tree cavities near water
entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. A diving duck of cold fast rivers; unmistakable sawtooth bill if the camera gets close.

entries.name: White stork
entries.migrates: migrates to Africa and India for the winter
behaviour: nests on chimneys, poles and church towers near wetlands
bill-clattering greeting ritual
soars in columns on thermals during migration

voxel_model.pattern: black flight feathers, red bill and legs

entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. Bringer of babies in European folklore; big stick nests on chimneys are a beloved landmark.

entries.name: Common kingfisher
behaviour: perches low over the water, dives headfirst at fish
excavates a tunnel nest in steep riverbanks
a flash of cobalt and orange past the player's shoulder

voxel_model.pattern: cobalt back, rust belly, white neck patch

entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. The river's gemstone; lives along clear, fish-rich streams and is visible only in flashes.

entries.name: White-throated dipper
behaviour: walks and swims underwater on fast headwater streams
bobs constantly on a rock before diving
builds domed moss nests under bridges and waterfalls

voxel_model.pattern: white throat and breast on dark body

entries.notes: gestation_days is incubation. The only songbird that dives and walks along streambeds; a reward for players who explore headwaters.

entries.name: Amazon river dolphin
entries.migrates: follows seasonal flood cycles into inundated forest
behaviour: pink as adults; grey when young
navigates by echolocation in muddy water
famously shy, but draws close to canoes
entries.notes: The boto of Amazonian myth; adults turn pink from abrasion and capillaries. Endangered, tied to the flooded-forest cycle. gestation_days is about 11 months.

entries.name: Indus river dolphin
behaviour: functionally blind; navigates by clicks aimed by a melon on the snout
swims tilted on one side
prefers shallow, murky, barrage-divided stretches
entries.notes: One of the world's rarest mammals, confined to the Indus by dams. 'Blind dolphin of the Indus'; a living symbol of a dammed river.

entries.name: Atlantic salmon
entries.migrates: anadromous: ocean-grown adults return to natal rivers to spawn
behaviour: leaps waterfalls and rapids on the spawning run
homing precision to the birth stream
some adults survive to spawn more than once

voxel_model.pattern: silvery parr with red spots turning olive on spawn

entries.notes: King of cold rivers; escaped-farmed hybrids do cross with wild fish. The leap upstream is the classic fishing-game moment.

entries.name: Sockeye salmon
entries.migrates: anadromous: returns to natal rivers and lakes to spawn
behaviour: spawning adults turn crimson with green heads
semelparous: dies after one spawning
fry rear in lakes before running to the sea

voxel_model.pattern: spawning fish: red body, green head

entries.notes: One life, one run. Dead carcasses after spawning feed the whole river forest; salmon runs move tens of thousands of tonnes of biomass.

entries.name: Northern pike
behaviour: ambush predator lurking in weed beds
duckling and vole specialist
cannibalistic; big pike eat smaller pike
entries.notes: The torpedo of cold weedy rivers; a favourite target for anglers and a natural check on fish populations.

entries.name: Common carp
behaviour: bottom-feeds, rooting the silt for food
large and golden-scaled; a farmed and game fish for 2000 years
turns muddy waters turbid
entries.notes: One of the world's most widespread freshwater fish thanks to millennia of farming; a staple food and a stubborn survivor.

entries.name: European eel
entries.migrates: catadromous: matures in rivers, migrates to the Sargasso Sea to spawn
behaviour: spawning ground never directly observed; millions converge on the Sargasso Sea
glass eels wash into estuaries in spring tides
can cross wet grass between waters
entries.notes: Critically endangered. Their life cycle was a mystery for millennia; nobody has ever seen an eel breed. A river's quiet mystery.

entries.name: Wels catfish
behaviour: lives in deep holes under banks and sunken trees
male guards the egg nest
takes ducklings off the surface; folklore exaggerated the man-eater
entries.notes: Europe's biggest freshwater fish, over 2.5 m on record, living up to 80 years. The stuff of river monsters; hook one at midnight.

entries.name: Capybara
behaviour: semi-aquatic; keeps nostrils and eyes just above the surface
hosts oxpeckers, ticks and even caiman-tolerant birds on its back
barks like a dog when alarmed
entries.notes: The world's largest rodent and the river's barnyard: fat, brown, social and famously unbothered, with birds perched on its back.

entries.name: Red-bellied piranha
behaviour: shoals for mutual defence; the feeding frenzy is mostly on carrion
serrated interlocking teeth shear flesh in single bites
nests in dug hollows guarded by both parents

voxel_model.pattern: red belly, silver flanks, dark spots when young

entries.notes: The horror-movie fish that mostly eats carrion and fruit; shoaling is about defence, not appetite. Still not a pleasant swim at dusk.

entries.name: Electric eel
behaviour: discharges 600+ volts to stun prey and deter threats
obligate air-breather; gulps the surface
leaps out of the water against threats, pressing its body to close the circuit
entries.notes: A living Taser from the Amazon floodplain. Despite the name it is a knifefish, not a true eel. Its leaping threat display is genuinely terrifying.

entries.name: Arapaima
behaviour: obligate air-breather; rises every few minutes to gulp air
one of the largest freshwater fish on Earth
bony-tongued, eats fish whole

voxel_model.pattern: dark body, red-edged tail and flanks

entries.notes: The 'red pirarucu' of the Amazon; air-breathing giant over 2 m long. Its scales were used as armour and its flesh feeds river towns.

entries.name: Alligator gar
behaviour: ancient lineage unchanged for millions of years
gulls air with a surfacing gulp
explosive ambush from the surface
entries.notes: A living fossil with needle teeth and one gulp of air; historically persecuted as a 'trash fish', now protected in several states.

entries.name: Paddlefish
entries.migrates: annual upriver runs to spawn in fast gravel
behaviour: swims open-mouth through clouds of plankton
long paddle rostrum packed with electroreceptors
historically dammed-river casualty; spawning runs fail behind dams
entries.notes: Mississippi-basin giant of the filter-feeding world; roe marketed as 'American caviar'. Dams have wrecked its runs.

entries.name: Mekong giant catfish
behaviour: gentle giant; the largest freshwater fish of Asia
slow-growing, matures after ~6 years
wild individuals now vanishingly rare
entries.notes: Critically endangered, possibly functionally extinct in the wild; adults over 200 kg once filled Mekong markets. A monument of a fish.

entries.name: Bull shark
entries.migrates: moves between sea and freshwater; rivers serve as nurseries
behaviour: osmoregulates to cruise far up freshwater rivers (Mississippi, Zambezi, Ganges, Amazon)
dull, tenacious aggression; responsible for many unprovoked bites
gives birth in rivers and estuaries

voxel_model.pattern: blunt snout, grey above, white below

entries.notes: The river shark: a 3-metre marine predator that patrols warm muddy freshwater. Ask the fishermen of the Ganges or the Mississippi.

entries.name: Green anaconda
behaviour: semi-aquatic ambush in swamp and slow river
mating balls of several males around one female
constricts prey, then swallows it whole

voxel_model.pattern: olive with black oval blotches and orange flank stripes

entries.notes: The heaviest snake on Earth; a 60-kg shadow in blackwater lagoons. Live-bearing, not egg-laying. Tales exceed the truth — barely.

entries.name: Amazon river turtle
entries.migrates: long upriver migrations to nest on beaches
behaviour: mass nesting events ('arribadas') on exposed sandbanks
females tag the same beach across decades
eggs harvested heavily by people; nests heavily guarded by volunteers
entries.notes: gestation_days is sand incubation. South America's largest freshwater turtle; one moonless night on one beach, every year, a hundred eggs per nest.

entries.name: Chinese giant salamander
behaviour: largest amphibian alive
ambush predator in cold mountain streams
named 'wa wa' for its cry, said to sound like a wailing baby
entries.notes: Critically endangered; once common in Chinese mountain streams, now mostly farmed. A living relic older than the dinosaurs' extinction.

entries.name: Water monitor
behaviour: strong swimmer and diver; disappears underwater with a flick of the tail
forked tongue tastes the air and the water
notorious raider of village chicken coops and fish ponds

voxel_model.pattern: yellow bands and spots on dark body

entries.notes: The crocodile-substitute of Asian rivers; common, bold, and mistaken for a small croc at a glance. Lays soft-shelled eggs in termite mounds.

entries.name: Common snapping turtle
behaviour: bottom-dwelling ambush predator
long tail sawtooth-crested
hauls ashore to nest in sandy banks in June
entries.notes: The tank-trap of the shallows; bites anything that steps on it. Respect the beak, and keep fingers clear of a hauling turtle.

entries.name: American bullfrog
behaviour: low foghorn bellow heard across ponds at night
ambush hunter on the bank edge
tadpoles take 2-3 years to metamorphose; invasive worldwide

voxel_model.pattern: mottled green; tympanum larger than eye in males

entries.notes: The foghorn of North American ponds; exported so widely for frog-legs that it now outcompetes native frogs across Europe and Asia.

entries.name: Noble crayfish
behaviour: burrows under banks and stones
walks backwards when alarmed
European native displaced by signal crayfish and crayfish plague
entries.notes: The native crayfish of European rivers, now scarce; if the player finds one, the river is in good health.
